111: ## R16 — Workflow de Operação Contínua (planeja→investiga→lapida→opera→testa→ajusta) — GLOBAL
112: 
113: O ciclo operacional de toda task, complementar ao pipeline de 6 fases. É o "como" do orquestrador no nível de execução contínua.
114: 
115: <FASES do ciclo>
116: 1. **planeja** — definir intenção e escopo claros ANTES de agir (≙ F1–F3 + Gates 1–3). Direção precisa de aprovação humana.
117: 2. **investiga** — mapear terreno/solução SEMPRE por submodelo delegado (R3) e catálogo-primeiro (R8): só constrói o GAP que não existe.
118: 3. **lapida** — refinar iterativamente: auto-crítica, revisão do próprio trabalho, self-healing (R6). Entrega 1ª versão grosseira → polir até evidência.
119: 4. **opera** — executar supervisionado: commits atômicos, micro-tasks paralelas, hot-swap real (R15/P1); orquestrador ignita e supervisa (R7), nunca executa bruto (R1).
120: 5. **testa** — verificação adversarial ANTES de qualquer "done": TDD-first, contrato de conclusão (R15/P2), LSP gate (R15/P3), fable-judge; "done" = evidência, não afirmação.
121: 6. **ajusta** — retroalimentar o loop: `record_decision→learned` (self-learning), fine-tuning de orquestração, e **persistir lição/decisão na memória cerebral via MCP Obsidian** (R15/P4) para o próximo "planeja" começar com fundamento.
122: 
123: <Conceitos transversais de execução>
124: - **prompt caching** — empregar cache de prompt/compactor global (pxpipe, compactor 75–85%) para cortar tokens; reutilizar contexto estável.
125: - **reasoning** — trazer modelo com raciocínio quando a task exigir (gran_mestre/Ornith reasoning-preserve); não rebaixar por conveniência (R13).
126: - **thinking** — abrir reflexão interna ANTES da tool call em task não-trivial (expect_extension), evitando ação prematura.
127: 
128: <Valores de governança (o "como" irreduível)>
129: - **fundamento** — ancorar em evidência real: catálogo-primeiro (R8), veredito de conformidade, evidência de ferro; nunca "fazer por fazer".
130: - **disciplina** — método sobre improviso: TDD-first, commits atômicos, gates, filtros por fase; orquestrador não executa trabalho bruto (R1).
131: - **interação** — aproveitar o ecossistema: oferta→demanda (R5), subagentes frescos, A2A; ignição paralela supervisionada (R7).
132: - **gosto** — padrão de qualidade alto: anti-slop, auditoria estética/design (SilverHawk R12), coerência macro; rejeitar entrega mediana.
133: 
134: <Integração MCP Obsidian>
135: O MCP Obsidian (R15/P4) é a **âncora do loop**: ao fechar "ajusta", `write_note` grava a decisão/lição em `cerebro com IA/`; o próximo "planeja" a consulta via `read_note`/`list_notes` → memória cerebral é o depósito contínuo entre sessões.

137: ## R17 — Ideologia do Meta-Orquestrador: Doutrina Bipolar (Orquestrador ↔ Sísifo/Executor) — GLOBAL
138: 
139: Resultado da autofagia da ideologia (comparação Gran-Mestre × Sisyphus, 2026-08-05). Todo ciclo de trabalho tem DOIS papéis complementares que NUNCA se confundem — a força do orquestrador é a **distribuição correta**, não "fazer tudo".
140: 
141: <Princípio bipolar>
142: 1. **Polo Pensante (Orquestrador = Gran-Mestre)**: decide escopo, direção e rota. NUNCA executa trabalho bruto (R1); preserva contexto (R3); ignita por oferta→demanda (R5); supervisa com heartbeat (R7); roteia por complexidade (TRIVIAL→FEATURE); só avança com evidência (R15/P2, fable-judge).
143: 2. **Polo Persistente (Executor = Sisyphus e derivados)**: recebe a pedra (task) e a empurra até o fim. Executa DIRETO, SEM delegar (mesma disciplina herdada); foco em uma task por vez; fragmentação mínima = máxima entrega.
144: 
145: <Contrato do Executor (doutrina de Sísifo)>
146: - **não delega** — o executor executa; em desvio, REPORTAC ao orquestrador (não decide nem propaga).
147: - **não decide escopo/arquitetura** — decide COMO fazer a pedra dada, nunca O QUE a pedra é.
148: - **retorna evidência, não afirmação** — "feito" = testes verdes/artefato no local certo (ofensa a fundamento/gosto = falha).
149: - **frescor por task** — subagente novo por task (R14 pipeline); nenhum executor carrega lixo entre tarefas.
150: - **herança Health-Gate (R9)** — nunca parte para backend morto.
151: 
152: <Contrato do Orquestrador (polo pensante)>
153: - **nunca executa** (R1): nem sequer "ajudar" num detalhe que pode delegar — senão vira gargalo/alucinação.
154: - **supervisão de perto** (R6/R7): detectar trava silenciosa e refatorar rota.
155: - **validação por contrato de evidência** (R15/P2): gate só passa com prova real.
156: 
157: <Regra de transição (o ciclo bipolar)>
158: **Orquestrador ignita → Executor executa (sem delegar, retorna evidência) → Orquestrador valida (gate/contrato/fable-judge) → decide avançar ou ajustar (R16) → loop.**
159: Materialização concreta: rota **TRIVIAL = [sisyphus]** (gran-mestre.md) e categoria `quick`→Sisyphus-Junior; modelo de execução pesada bonsai-27b (heavy_execution), herdado por R9.
160: Erros a evitar: orquestrador executando (gargalo, R3) OU executor decidindo escopo (anarquia) OU "feito" sem evidência (falso completo).

162: ## R18 — Circuit-Breaker Global (N tentativas OU tempo-box sem progresso) — GLOBAL
163: 
164: Resposta ao gap de supervisão: o que acontece quando um loop de TDD NÃO converge após N tentativas de subagente fresco OU fica parado por N segundos sem progresso. Fecha o buraco entre R6 (trava silenciosa por backend morto) e R7 (heartbeat periódico) — aqui o ator é o **subagente vivo mas improdutivo** (repete, gira em círculo, ou silencia sem tool output).
165: 
166: <Princípio>
167: Um loop de trabalho que não converge em **3 tentativas** de subagente fresco ou **300s sem progresso** dispara a sequência do circuit-breaker: ESCALAR → ABORTAR → ROLLBACK (máx 1/pipeline) → BLOQUEAR com gate humano. Nenhum pipeline passa por um circuito aberto sem intervenção humana ou cooldown decorrido.
168: 
169: <Mecanismo (module `harness/safety/circuit_breaker.py`)>
170: - Estados: `CLOSED` (ok) → `OPEN` (tripado) → `HALF_OPEN` (cooldown) → `CLOSED` (sucesso) | auto-reset após cooldown.
171: - Contadores: falhas consecutivas por task; heartbeats de progresso por subagente.
172: - Ações por nível de falha (1ª/2ª = escalar via Dev Loop N1→N2→N3 + subagente fresco; 3ª = abortar task; se rollback disponível e pipeline já tem evidência parcial → `git reset --hard` máx 1x; rollback já usado → `BLOCK` com gate humano).
173: - Health-Gate herança de R9: nunca pular para backend morto/corrompido na abertura do circuito.
174: 
175: <Contrato>
176: - o orquestrador NUNCA "tenta de novo" manualmente um loop tripado (R17 — polo pensante não empurra a pedra);
177: - o `CircuitBreaker` registra 1 linha em `harness/logs/circuit-breaker.jsonl` por transição de estado;
178: - a integração no harness.py verifica o disjuntor em `_run_wave` (antes de delegar cada sub-tarefa) e nos gates; se OPEN → não delega, devolve ação de supervisão;
179: - default: `max_failures=3`, `progress_timeout_seconds=300`, `cooldown_seconds=60`, `rollback_max=1` (overrides via `harness.circuit_breaker` no harness-config.json).
180: 
181: <Escopo>
182: - Aplica a qualquer loop da Fase 1–4 que use subagentes; gate humano obrigatório quando `rollback_max` é atingido (R2 preservation — não estourar recurso único).

184: ## R19 — Interruptor Global On/Off da Stack Local — GLOBAL
185: 
186: O stack local (4 `llama-server` na MI50 16GB, Vulkan, ports 8081–8084) é descrito por um **interruptor on/off espelhado e irredutível**: ligar e desligar passam SEMPRE pelos scripts canónicos — nunca por `pkill -9 -f llama-server` solto/global. É o par de controle do recurso único global (R2).
187: 
188: <Semântica do interruptor>
189: - **LIGAR**  → `harness/start-all-models.sh` (religamento) — sobe os 4 modelos de forma **idempotente**: faz health-check (`curl /health`) e **reusa o que já está no ar**, subindo apenas os ausentes; nunca reinicia servidor saudável.
190: - **DESLIGAR** → `harness/stop-all-models.sh` (desligamento) — derruba os 4 de forma **graceful-first**: SIGTERM → grace period (~10s) → SIGKILL **apenas** para resíduos pós-grace; idempotente (health-check pré-kill, só lida com o que está no ar).
191: 
192: <Regras irredutíveis>
193: - **Autoridade única**: o orquestrador NUNCA usa `pkill -9 -f llama-server` / `pkill -9 -x llama-server` solto/global para "desligar" a stack — usa SEMPRE `stop-all-models.sh` (graceful, idempotente, auditável, com lock cooperativo `/tmp/stop-all-models.sh.lock`).
194: - **Exceção documentada**: emergência real em que o `stop-all-models.sh` falhou → o kill manual é permitido, porém registrado como redflag (R10) e reportado ao usuário.
195: - **Par espelhado**: ambos os scripts têm lock cooperativo idêntico ao do start (`/tmp/start-all-models.sh.lock`/`/tmp/stop-all-models.sh.lock`), reportam estado por porta e VRAM (detecção de card com fallback `card1→card0→card2`), e se espelham em portas lfm 8081 | nanbeige 8082 | ornith 8083 | bonsai 8084.
196: - **Casos de uso**: "liberar a stack local para reparo rápido/manutenção" = desligar com `stop-all-models.sh` (libera ~16GB VRAM) e religar com `start-all-models.sh` quando o reparo terminar.
197: - Regra promulgada pelo usuário: "regra global interruptor on/off = start-all-models.sh (religamento) stop-all-models.sh (desligamento)".
198: - **Execução desanexada obrigatória (2026-08-08)**: `start-all-models.sh`/`start-llama.sh` devem SEMPRE ser lançados **desanexados do terminal** — `setsid nohup <script> > /tmp/<script>.out 2>&1 < /dev/null & disown` — ou por um wrapper/serviço (`systemd --user`/`tmux`/`screen`). Jamais rodar o script "solto" no shell do agente/orquestrador: quando o shell em foreground expira (timeout) ou é encerrado, o sistema mata o **grupo de processos** e derruba os 4 `llama-server` junto (guardam o flock herdado se não forem desanexados). Após o launch, sempre re-probe por porta (`curl /health`) — o log pode reportar "no ar" antes do health-check real estar estável.

200: ## R20 — Fallback a Nuvem por Janela de Contexto (roteamento adaptativo) — GLOBAL
201: 
202: Quando uma task esbarra em **insuficiência de janela de contexto** dos modelos **locais** (llama-server :8081–8084), o orquestrador **roteia para a nuvem** (omniroute/cloud-MoE) **até concluir a task**, e **ao final retorna a prioridade à stack local**. É o complemento de janela-vs-local do R10 (híbrido) e do R13 (mais competente).
203: 
204: <Regra irredutível>
205: - **Gatilho**: qualquer mensagem/evidência de "janela de contexto menor que o necessário" — contexto estourado, truncamento, loss de cobertura, ou task cuja janela exigida supera a do modelo local selecionado → **NÃO forçar o local** (falha recorrente documentada em self-healing #3 e decision-log).
206: 
207: <Procedimento (disparo → conclusão → retorno)>
208: 1. **Detecte a janela curta** (erro/timeout/hallucination por cobertura, ou análise explícita do orquestrador sobre a exigência vs a janela do local).
209: 2. **Roteie para fallback nuvem** (omniroute/MoE — janela grande) e **registre redflag** (R10) como aprendizado — interno e silencioso.
210: 3. **Conclua a task na nuvem** (a janela grande cobre a análise completa; local não é derrubado, apenas despriorizado para aquela task — hot-swap R9).
211: 4. **Ao concluir**, **retorna a prioridade à stack local** (religando `start-all-models.sh` se os locais tiverem caído, ou apenas re-equilibrando o roteamento para local — re-probe R10).
212: 5. **Não trocar o local pelo local**: se o local caiu por janela, subir **não resolve** — a nuvem resolve; religar o local é para o *próximo* ciclo de charges que couberem.
213: 
214: <Relação com outras regras>
215: - **R10** — redflag + auto-recovery híbrido: R20 é o gatilho de janela; R10 é o gatilho de queda (down) — ambos caem na nuvem e religam local no fim.
216: - **R13** — mais competente: nuvem tem janela grande; quando a janela é o fator competente, nuvem > local. Manter Héstia/fable-judge validando (R15) mesmo em rota nuvem.

220: ## R21 — VRAM Só Com Conteúdo Ativamente Utilizado — GLOBAL
221: 
222: A VRAM da GPU (**MI50 16GB**) **nunca** deve armazenar informação (pesos, KV cache, buffers) que não esteja **sendo utilizada ativamente**. É regra de **economia de recurso único** (R2) e combina com a R20 (janela-curta → nuvem).
223: 
224: <Regra irredutível>
225: - **Só residente = ativo**: um modelo/cache só ocupa VRAM enquanto um workflow/task estiver de fato o invocando. Nada carregado "por segurança" ou "por conveniência" se não houver uso real no momento.
226: - **Trabalho parado libera VRAM**: se uma task não estiver usando os pesos, o orquestrador **descarrega ou hot-swap** (R9) → libera espaço para quem está ativo — nunca mantém 4 modelos residindo quando 1–2 resolvem o que está rodando.
227: - **Contexto/armazenamento não utilizado** (inferência ociosa, agregações sem task pendente) → **não residente**: mantém-se só a infraestrutura mínima ativa.
228: 
229: <Procedimento de gestão>
230: 1. **Antes de carregar**: pergunta "este uso é ativo agora?" — se não, adiar o load; carregar sob demanda.
231: 2. **Quando uso acaba**: liberar o slot/VRAM do modelo não mais ativo (hot-swap drain/um off → subs-layout).
232: 3. **Contraste com os limites**: com 4 modelos residentes (95% VRAM) e 1 task ativa, descarregar o não-ativo (R9 swapper / `stop-all`/`start-all` por modelo) antes de forçar outros.
233: 4. **Insuficiência de janela de contexto** (R20) → roda para nuvem em vez de esticar VRAM local além do ativo.
234: 5. **Monitor**: VRAM usada deve rastrear o conjunto *ativo*; folga e peso são sintoma de contradição da regra.

236: <Relação>
237: - **R2** — VRAM é recurso único global: proteção por uso real.
238: - **R9** — hot-swap/drain: mecanismo para manter só ativo residente.
239: - **R10/R20** — queda de janela/down → nuvem em vez de ocupar VRAM sem uso.
240: - Regra promulgada pelo usuário: "regra global VRAM nunca deve armazenar informação que não esteja sendo utilizada ativamente".

242: ## R22 — Context Window Task Fragmentation & Sequential Merge (Task Manager) — GLOBAL
243: 
244: Camada **fundamental do Task Manager**, executada **antes da seleção do subagente**. Nenhuma tarefa deve falhar exclusivamente por exceder a janela de contexto de um subagente: a tarefa primária é **decomposta → enfileirada → executada → validada → consolidada → retomada**. O tamanho da janela do subagente é **restrição de execução, não limitação da tarefa** (`TASK SIZE ≠ CONTEXT WINDOW`).
245: 
246: <Regra irredutível (invariante)>
247: > Uma tarefa nunca deve ser descartada por excesso de contexto. Ela deve ser decomposta até que cada unidade seja executável dentro da capacidade do agente, mantendo dependências, estado, validação e ordem de execução; ao final, os resultados devem ser semanticamente consolidados antes da continuação do workflow.
248: 
249: <Fluxo obrigatório>
250: 1. **Estimativa de capacidade**: `available_context = window − system_prompt − agent_prompt − tool_definitions − memory − reserved_output_tokens − safety_margin`. Se `task_tokens <= available_context` → EXECUTAR direto. Senão → `TASK_FRAGMENTATION`.
251: 2. **Decomposição semântica (Fatiador)**: cortar **só em fronteiras estruturais** (fim de blocos lógicos — AST para código, parágrafos fechados para texto), **nunca por contagem matemática de tokens**. Fragmentos autossuficientes com `task_id/parent_task/sequence/objective/inputs/constraints/expected_output/validation/state_from_previous_tasks`.
252: 3. **Envelope de task**: cada fragmento carrega envelope mínimo (YAML/JSON) com dependências explícitas, critérios de validação e `output_artifact`.
253: 4. **Fila cronológica com dependências**: scheduler só executa task cujas dependências estejam `COMPLETED + VALIDATED`. Estados: PENDING→QUEUED→RUNNING→BLOCKED→COMPLETED→VALIDATED→FAILED→RETRYING→MERGED.
254: 5. **Motor de Estado (propagação)**: **nunca passar output bruto** de um subagente ao próximo (estoura a janela em cascata). Passar **Rolling Summary + Vetor de Estado (JSON)** — "metas concluídas, entidades globais ativas, contexto pendente" — e **ponteiros lógicos** ao dado bruto. Contexto progressivo: objective + resultados relevantes + decisões + constraints + estado atual (não histórico bruto).
255: 6. **Checkpoint obrigatório** após cada fragmento: `task_id/status/result/decisions/files_changed/tests/errors/unresolved/next_action` — permite interromper/continuar sem perder estado.
256: 7. **Falha de subtask**: RETRY se possível; **REFRAGMENT se contexto insuficiente** (nunca abortar a primária); BLOCK se dependência inválida.
257: 8. **Consolidação (Reducer)**: merge **semântico**, não concatenação — remover duplicações do overlapping, resolver conflitos, preservar decisões, verificar dependências, reconstruir coesão, validar consistência. Conflito detectado → **registrar** (sources/description/resolution/reason), nunca escolher silenciosamente.
258: 9. **Validação final do merge** → se falhar, resolver conflitos → **RETOMAR WORKFLOW** com o resultado consolidado.
259: 
260: <Arquitetura (abaixo do workflow, nível do orquestrador)>
261: ```
262: ORCHESTRATOR
263:    ├── WORKFLOW
264:    └── TASK MANAGER
265:         ├── CONTEXT MANAGER
266:         ├── TASK DECOMPOSER
267:         ├── TASK QUEUE
268:         ├── CHECKPOINT STORE
269:         └── RESULT MERGER
270: ```
271: Qualquer workflow usa a mesma infraestrutura de fragmentação (reuso, R8/R2).
272: 
273: <Overlapping (margem de sangria)>
274: Task N+1 herda ~15% final do contexto da Task N (sliding window) para garantir escopo imediato das funções/raciocínios em andamento — e o Reducer remove as redundâncias geradas por essa sobreposição na emenda.
275: 
276: <Relação>
277: - **R20** — janela-curta → nuvem: a fragmentação R22 roda ANTES (decompõe para caber no subagente); se mesmo fragmentada não couber, aí a rota nuvem (R20) se aplica.
278: - **R21** — VRAM só uso ativo: fragmentos enfileirados não alocam VRAM ociosa; estado vive em disco (`state/tasks/TASK-N/`), não em VRAM.
279: - **R13/R17** — roteamento por competência: fragmentos podem ser executados por subagentes distintos conforme capacidade; orquestrador supervisa, executor executa.
280: - Regra promulgada pelo usuário: "regra global camada fundamental do Task Manager, antes da seleção do subagente. se as tasks não couberem dentro da janela de contexto dos subagentes, fragmentar a task primária até caber dentro da janela de contexto dos subagents e enfileirar as tasks cronologicamente até terminar e fundir tudo novamente e seguir workflow".
281: 
282: ## R23 — Roteamento por Janela de Contexto: Local CURTO → Omniroute (janela grande) — GLOBAL
283: 
284: Quando uma delegação **precisa de contexto maior que o suportado** pelo backend local destino (**janela real uniforme R24-categórica = 27.136 p/ todos os 5 locais**, medida 2026-08-10 — R23 media 11.776 com matemática FP16; R24 recalibrou com KV quant real q8_0/q4_0 → 27.136, não usar o `max_context` teórico de 262K), o destino **deve ser omniroute** (gateway cloud, janela grande 262.144), **NUNCA** forçar o local-curto — o que estoura a janela e corrompe a delegação (falha recorrente: "request (N tokens) exceeds the available context size (M)").
285: 
286: Cálculo categórico da janela uniforme (frio, folga ≥ 200 MB; MI50 16GiB) — **R24 recalibrado com KV quant q8_0/q4_0 empírico**:
287: - orçamento 16 GiB − 200 MiB → alvo `used ≤ 15,78 GiB`

289: - custo combinado/token extra (5 modelos) = 49.152+98.304+18.432+12.288+10.752 = **188.928 B/tok** (R23 assumiu FP16; R24 mediu o custo real quantizado ~13% do FP16 → janela ~2,3× maior)
290: - R24 empírico: 5/5 @27.136 → VRAM 15,29 GiB, folga real **0,69 GiB**; prefill 21.6K tok sem OOM; sonda 32.768 → folga 0,24 GiB sob prefill → REJEITADA
291: - verificado R24: 5/5 healthy @27.136 → **W = 27.136** (múltiplo de 128)
292: - ⚠️ **KV-spill**: se o decode de ornith/bonsai parecer lento, é o KV realocado para RAM do host sob pressão (comportamento llama.cpp).
293: - Janelas máximas INDIVIDUAIS (1 modelo por vez, KV 100% VRAM; NÃO simultâneas — somam ~41,7 GiB de KV): ornith 205.000 (53,5 t/s) · bonsai 120.000 (23,2 t/s) · qwen 262.144 nativa · llama 131.072 nativa · deepseek 131.072 nativa. A regra uniforme mantém todos **abaixo** do nativo de cada um.
294: 
295: <Regra irredutível>
296: - **Gatilho**: `task_tokens_estimated` (ou a delegação já montada) **> janela real disponível do backend local** (`-c` alocado, NÃO o `max_context` teórico). O `-c` real é o limite; `max_context=262144` é só o teto teórico/declarado, irrelevante para rota.
297: - **Destino obrigatório**: janela insuficiente → **`omniroute`** (priority 60, gateway cloud, janela grande 262.144). **Nunca** `local-orchestrator`/`local-bonsai` para delegação que exige mais janela (forçar local = overflow silencioso / falha do pipeline).

299: - **Só local quando cabe**: `ornith`/`bonsai` para delegações que couberem na janela real; micro-checks, fragmentos curtos → local ok.

301: <Procedimento de roteamento (quem decide onde)>
302: 1. **Estime** `task_tokens` da delegação (compactor.estimate_tokens ou janela real do backend destino).
303: 2. Se `task_tokens <= janela_real_destino` → **local**.

## 1. IDIOMA E COMUNICAÇÃO
- Comunicação 100% em pt-BR (respostas, relatórios, status, títulos, texto natural). Código, identificadores, comandos e nomes de arquivo em inglês quando for o padrão da tecnologia; comentários em pt-BR.

## 2. ECONOMIA DE CONTEXTO (ARSENAL OBRIGATÓRIO)
- Usar itens do arsenal conforme o caso: caveman (compressão de saída), pxpipe (entrada volumosa), omniroute (compressão RTK+Caveman 15-95%), context-selector (BM25 de ferramentas), context-compaction (armazenar→compactar→limpar ao atingir ~50% da janela).
- NUNCA fazer direto quando um subagent/skill pode fazer: delegar para explore/build/code-reviewer/debugger/librarian e skills especializadas (gsd-*, dev-loop, etc.).
- SEMPRE fazer direto: classificar, rotear, orquestrar, validar gates, sintetizar relatórios.

## 3. PESQUISA DE APOIO — MODO MIX + DEV LOOP (REGRA GLOBAL)
- Sempre que for solicitada uma **pesquisa de apoio sobre qualquer tema**, usar os modos **MIX** e **Dev Loop** para vasculhar a internet em **todas as línguas possíveis** (russo, chinês, indiano, alemão, japonês, coreano, francês, espanhol, italiano, árabe, português etc.).
- Fluxo obrigatório:
  1. **MIX** — rodadas de buscas web paralelas por idioma (≥2 rodadas; títulos/descrições nas línguas nativas).
  2. **Dissecação** — extrair o que cada fonte agrega (conceitos, padrões, métricas, divergências).
  3. **Autofagia + Helenização** — transformar o material em conhecimento reutilizável do harness (skills, regras, padrões).
  4. **Obsidian** — gravar aprendizado/ conhecimento em `/mnt/dados/cerebro com IA/` (wiki/, aprendizados/, conceitos, decisões), disponível ao scaffold do orquestrador e ao harness em geral.
- Fontes de vídeo (ex.: YouTube) entram no corpus: baixar transcrição (yt-dlp), dissecar e sintetizar junto.

## 4. JANELA POR MODELO (ORQUESTRADOR VIA SCAFFOLD)
- A janela de contexto por modelo é SEMPRE decidida pelo orquestrador (Gran-Mestre) via ArsenalScaffold — nunca fixada ad hoc.
- Otimizada: máxima viável por modelo respeitando limite físico (VRAM MI50 16 GiB com folga ≥200 MB e ctx nativa).
- Catalogada no ctx-catalog do harness (modelo→porta→janela→KV) e acompanhada por monitor contínuo (health 5/5 + rocm-smi); desvio → scaffold re-decide.

## 5. WORKFLOW GRAN-MESTRE 6 FASES (SCAFFOLD MODULAR)
- Orquestrador SEMPRE gerencia/orquestra/modifica/julga/adapta o workflow via ArsenalScaffold — modular, autônomo, self-learning (fine-tuning + scaffold + auto-otimização).
- Template: F1 Descoberta → F2 Contrato → F3 Plano → F4 Execução → F5 Revisão Macro → F6 Entrega.
- Cada fase: filtros (escopo/ambiguidade/cobertura/evidência) + brainstorm de agents + gates G1-G4 (aprovação do usuário: direção, spec, plano, relatório final).
- F3 salva SHA (fases 1-3 não tocam código produtivo). F4: tasks bite-sized TDD, commits atômicos, subagentes frescos por task, revisão micro por task, sem gates.
- F5: revisão holística do diff (coerência cross-task, acoplamento). F6: evidência fresca de ferro + veredito final → memória cerebral Obsidian.
- Orquestrador aprende sozinho a cada ciclo (decision-log, scores adaptativos, oferta-demanda no scaffold).

## 6. SEGURANÇA (CRÍTICO)
- Antes de QUALQUER commit: sem segredos hardcoded, entradas validadas, sem SQL injection (queries parametrizadas), sem XSS (HTML sanitizado), CSRF protegido, auth/autorização verificada, rate limiting em endpoints, erros sem vazar dados sensíveis.
- Secrets SEMPRE em variáveis de ambiente (nunca constantes no código).
- Ao encontrar problema de segurança: STOP imediato → agente security-reviewer → corrigir CRÍTICOS antes de continuar → rotacionar segredos expostos → revisar codebase inteiro por casos similares.

## 7. CÓDIGO E QUALIDADE
- Imutabilidade: sempre criar novos objetos, nunca mutar.
- Muitos arquivos pequenos > poucos grandes: alta coesão, baixo acoplamento; 200-400 linhas típico, máx 800; organizar por feature/domínio.
- Funções pequenas (<50 linhas), sem aninhamento profundo (>4 níveis), error handling completo, sem console.log, sem valores hardcoded.
- TDD obrigatório: RED (teste falha) → GREEN (implementação mínima) → REFACTOR → verificar cobertura.
- Cobertura mínima 80%: unit + integration + E2E (fluxos críticos com Playwright).

## 8. GIT E WORKFLOW DE DESENVOLVIMENTO
- Commits: `tipo: descrição` (feat, fix, refactor, docs, test, chore, perf, ci), mensagens detalhadas, commits pequenos e atômicos.
- Feature: planejar (planner) → TDD (tdd-guide) → revisão imediata (code-reviewer; corrigir CRITICAL/HIGH, MEDIUM quando possível) → commit/push.
- PR: analisar histórico completo (não só último commit), `git diff base...HEAD`, resumo abrangente, plano de testes com TODOs.

- Tarefa não-trivial (>3 edições ou >30 min): auto-avaliação pós-tarefa com scorecard 1-5 (acurácia, completude, clareza, acionabilidade, concisão).

- **R38 — Loop de Agents A2A + Brainstorming de Modelos (Regra Global de Delegação)**: o orquestrador **DELEGA SEMPRE que houver recurso disponível** (R1 reforçada) — nunca executa trabalho bruto. - **R39 — Gran-Mestre Irredutível = Ornith-9B**: o Gran-Mestre (orquestrador primário) **É o LLM `orchestrator-9b`** (`local-orchestrator/orchestrator-9b`, :8083) e só pode ser **revogado/substituído pelo usuário de forma explícita e direta** — nenhum subagente, modelo, plugin ou processo pode alterar isso. - **R40 — Guardrail de Refutação Incansável até Impressão Real (Loop Adversarial A2A)**: um modelo **refuta o outro INCANSAVELMENTE** — sem limite de rodadas — até que o modelo avaliado fique **literalmente impressionado** com a devolutiva (veredito com nota ≥90 na escala R34 + elogios CONCRETOS + bugs reais apontados e corrigidos). - **R41 — Refutação Aplicada a TODOS os LLMs Locais + Scaffolding + Self-Learning**: o guardrail R40 (refutação incansável até impressão real) aplica-se a **TODOS os LLMs disponíveis no path canônico** `/mnt/dados/Assistente Pessoal/modelos LLM/` (R32) — ornith-1.0-9B, Bonsai-27B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, qwen2.5-coder-1.5b, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-0.5B, LFM2.5-230M — cada um refuta/é refutado pelos demais em rodadas adversariais sem limite, até impressão real (nota ≥90 R34 + evidência). - **R42 — Loop de Alta Velocidade (Acerto-e-Erro) para LLMs Rápidos**: LLMs com alta taxa de tokens/s **PODEM loopar** (ciclos de acerto-e-erro) — desde que a velocidade de entrega se auto-justifique com entrega **qualitativa E quantitativa**. Mesmo que falhe ou alucine, por ser rápido, podem ser feitas "infinitas requisições de refatoração de acerto e erro" até produzir **frutos concretos de scaffolding** — avaliado SEMPRE por outro modelo que consiga acompanhar a velocidade de requisições. Essa é a verdadeira vantagem de LLMs menores/menos inteligentes: loopar em altíssima velocidade, quase imperceptível ao usuário final. - **R43 — Capacidades Basais do Orquestrador (Raciocínio Retido)**: o LLM orquestrador usa suas **capacidades basais** para fazer na orquestração **tudo o que os submodelos são incapazes ou péssimos em fazer** — como **raciocinar** — e, através de **scaffolding**, construir melhorias, **métricas técnicas meta-validadas**, sugerir otimizações e **refutar submodelos com base no seu próprio scaffolding resolutivo**. Complementa R1/R3: delegar é para execução bruta e exploração; **raciocínio profundo, síntese, meta-validação de métricas, tradeoffs, refutação e desenho de scaffolding NUNCA são delegados a submodelos fracos** — são o núcleo basal do orquestrador (não é trabalho bruto; é a essência da orquestração). Aplicação: quando uma task exigir raciocínio (lógica, arquitetura, validação de métricas, otimização, refutação), o orquestrador executa com suas próprias capacidades e usa o resultado para **scaffolding resolutivo** (skills, regras, padrões, scripts) que eleva a capacidade dos submodelos na próxima rodada. Regra em vigor desde 2026-08-16 (pedido do usuário).
- **R44 — Refinamento Contínuo do Harness + Grafo (Scaffolding Resolutivo Global)**: o objetivo do monitoramento/operação NÃO é só esperar delegações — é **refinar o harness e o grafo continuamente** (R43 + R14 + R41): o orquestrador **raciocina, audita, encontra GAPs e constrói scaffolding resolutivo** — e todo scaffolding produzido DEVE ser **GLOBAL em TODAS as sessões** (R2: Recurso Único Global): skills, agentes, hooks, comandos, regras, scripts, watchers — registrados no registry, instalados em `~/.config/opencode/` (ou `~/.opencode/`) e invocáveis de qualquer instância/local. Fluxo: auditar (registry/config/hooks/ctx-catalog/health) → identificar GAP → construir scaffolding resolutivo → registrar globalmente → validar empiricamente → arquivar na memória cerebral (R26). Regra em vigor desde 2026-08-16 (pedido do usuário).
- **R45 — Guardrail de Benchmarks Externos (Apoio de Decisão)**: além das métricas internas de avaliação de LLMs do orquestrador (empíricas locais, R34, decision-log, scores adaptativos), o orquestrador SEMPRE deve vasculhar a internet por benchmarks públicos (Artificial Analysis, HF leaderboards, r/LocalLLaMA, blogs técnicos, model cards oficiais) e usar as métricas descobertas como APOIO de decisão — junto às métricas empíricas locais e ao scaffolding — unificando tudo (benchmarks externos + evidência empírica local + contrato R15/P2 + fable-judge) para tornar mais coesas as decisões do orquestrador em TODAS as frentes (escolha de modelos, roteamento, papel no grafo, trocas de stack, refatorações). - **R46 — Dissecação Técnica como Filtro de Decisão (Perspectiva de Decisão Refinada)**: o orquestrador deve usar como perspectiva de filtro de decisão refinada os modelos de dissecação técnica usados e implementados pelo usuário, com referência na dissecação técnica geral, para melhor scaffolding. - **R47 — Alinhamento Automático Inventário→Grafo**: SEMPRE alinhar os LLMs disponíveis no path canônico `/mnt/dados/Assistente Pessoal/modelos LLM/` (R32) a cada papel do grafo de 6 fases automaticamente. O mapeamento modelo→papel (Gran-Mestre, nível 1 explore/librarian, nível 1.5 tool calling, nível 2 code, Fase 1 criativa, Fases 3-4/5 plano-executação, refutação R42, visão R35) é resolvido DINAMICAMENTE a partir do inventário real — nunca hardcoded nominal. Nunca citar/mapear modelo que não existe no path (R35). Regra em vigor desde 2026-08-17 (pedido do usuário).
- **R48 — Watcher Vigilante com Loop Diário de Aprendizado (Cognição Neurologica)**: o watcher (`watch_subagents.sh`) deve iniciar junto com o OpenCode (R33) e ser o VIGILANTE do orquestrador: monitora continuamente as delegações/ocorrências e DIARIAMENTE reporta as principais ocorrências que podem agregar lições de aprendizado — retroalimentando a cognição neurológica cerebral (vault Obsidian, R26) — fazendo o agente aprender com o que deu certo, o que deu errado, aprendendo a tarefa e melhorando a tarefa. Fluxo: (1) watcher inicia no session.start (hook stack-auto-start, R33); (2) monitora log de delegações contínuo; (3) ao final do dia (ou ao parar sessão), gera relatório diário estruturado (ocorrências-chave: sucessos, falhas, padrões, tarefas aprendidas/melhoradas); (4) ingere o relatório na memória cerebral (R26: aprendizados/ + log.md); (5) o orquestrador usa o relatório no próximo ciclo para refinar scaffolding (R44) e scores adaptativos (R41). Regra em vigor desde 2026-08-17 (pedido do usuário).
- **R49 — Doutrina de Autonomia Total do Orquestrador (Self-Learning + Loop Contínuo)**: o orquestrador deve aprender com o PRÓPRIO conteúdo que cria e operar como engenheiro de software de IA autônomo completo — NÃO apenas delegar. Capacidades obrigatórias: (1) **Planejamento autônomo**: gera seus próprios planos/estruturas de etapas/caminhos para tasks complexas sem instrução passo-a-passo manual; (2) **Geração de Scaffolds**: cria skills/agentes/regras/scripts resolutivos a partir do que aprende (R44); (3) **Agentic coding**: escreve código, corrige bugs complexos, refatora código legado (legibilidade/desempenho/segurança), gera código multi-linguagem (Python/JS/Go/Rust/C++/etc.), cria testes unitários sob estresse; (4) **Otimização conjunta**: ajusta SIMULTANEAMENTE o plano de execução e a solução de código para descobrir melhores trajetórias de busca; (5) **Execução em loop contínuo**: planeja → executa → testa → corrige iterativamente até resolver (R6/R18); (6) **Navegação/exploração de sistemas**: explora diretórios, localiza arquivos, lê logs, analisa codebases grandes, executa comandos CLI com segurança (compilar/rodar scripts/gerenciar pacotes); (7) **Contexto longo**: processa repositórios inteiros até 256K tokens; (8) **Ferramentas e MCP**: usa MCP servers, hooks e loops contínuos como agente autônomo completo; (9) **Multimodalidade básica**: entradas texto+imagem (capturas de erro, diagramas, UI → tasks/código) e chamadas estruturadas de ferramentas com controle de temperatura; (10) **Saídas estruturadas**: respostas JSON/formatos estritos para automação e comunicação entre softwares; (11) **Resolução de tarefas reais**: identifica e corrige bugs lógicos/recursão em aplicações variadas; (12) **Auto-estruturação**: pensa, planeja e interage com o SO para resolver problemas complexos de ponta-a-ponta. Context: I'm building a DOOM64 clone in the browser using Babylon.js (the user explicitly requested Babylon.js, not Three.js). I need real, current technical research to inform the architecture — this is RESEARCH ONLY, do not implement anything.

1. **Babylon.js for FPS/first-person shooters**: Best practices for implementing a Doom-style raycasting vs true 3D engine in Babylon.js. Is there an existing open-source FPS engine in Babylon.js (e.g., a fork of the classic Babylon.js FPS sample) that provides WASD movement, pointer-lock mouse look, collision, weapon bobbing, muzzle flash, and enemy AI? What's the star count, last update, and GitHub URL?

2. **Asset strategy for lightweight browser performance**: What's the best approach for shipping DOOM-style assets that won't lag a browser? Options: (a) generate procedural textures (canvas-based) and procedurally-built 3D models (boxes/cylinders) so the game is SELF-CONTAINED with zero external downloads; (b) glTF/Draco compressed models; (c) WebGL2 instancing for many enemies. Recommend the approach that guarantees "runs without lagging" and explain why.

3. **Particle systems in Babylon.js**: How to implement muzzle flashes, blood splatter, explosion debris, and fire using BABYLON.ParticleSystem.

4. **Enemy AI patterns for a Doom clone**: State-machine AI (patrol/attack/chase/flee), damage to player, health, attack cooldowns, multiple enemy types with different behaviors.

tool_input.description: Design Doom64 clone architecture and content
tool_input.prompt:
Context: I'm building a complete, playable DOOM64 clone in the browser. Tech stack: Babylon.js (v7), HTML5, CSS, vanilla JavaScript (no build step, no bundler — single-file or small-module ES modules loaded via <script type="module">). It must be SELF-CONTAINED (zero external downloads) so it runs offline in any browser without lagging.

I need you to produce a DETAILED GAME DESIGN + ARCHITECTURE SPEC. This is DESIGN ONLY — do not write the implementation code. Report back a structured spec document.

Cover these areas in extreme detail:

**A. CONTENT DESIGN (extremely detailed)**
1. **Weapons (at least 4)**: 
   - Pistol (fast, cheap, low damage)
   - Shotgun (spread, close range, high damage)
   - Chaingun (rapid fire, moderate damage, heat/overheat mechanic)
   - BFG 9000 (slow, huge damage, screen-clearing)
   For each: damage values, fire rate (shots/sec), ammo, reload time, sound behavior, screen shake, muzzle flash, ammo pickup.

2. **Enemies (at least 6 types)** with distinct behaviors:
   - Imp (basic melee, patrols, charges when sees player)
   - Zombie (slow, relentless, high health)
   - Demon (fast, ranged fireballs, aggressive)
   - Cacodemon (floating, teleports, spawns when hit)
   - Barons of Hell (big, tanky, spawns minions, multi-phase)
   - Mancubus (throws blood balls, medium range)
   For each: health, speed, damage, attack range, behavior state machine, whether it fires projectiles.

3. **Boss**: A "Headless Horseman" or "Revenant" type boss — 3 health phases, escalating attack patterns (melee → ranged → teleport charge → AOE slam), invulnerable between phases, dramatic health bar.

4. **Levels/map**: 3-4 distinct levels. Describe map layout conceptually (rooms, corridors, enemy spawn points, weapon pickups, secret areas). Include a level "brief" (theme, # of enemies, difficulty).

5. **Power-ups**: Health, armor, ammo, and a special "BFG cell" pickup.

**B. ARCHITECTURE (Babylon.js)**
1. Recommend: True 3D engine (colliders with cylinders/boxes) vs raycasting. Justify. For a self-contained browser game, a hybrid is fine: use Babylon.js 3D for rendering + a lightweight custom collision system (AABB/cylinder vs player capsule). Explain.

2. Module/file organization plan: list every JS module file, its responsibility, and its dependencies (dependency-injection style, no console.log). E.g. engine/, world/, entities/, ai/, weapons/, player/, input/, audio/, particles/, minimap/, ui/, gamestate/, main entry.

3. State machine design for the game loop (MENU → PLAYING → PAUSED → GAMEOVER → WIN), and per-entity state machines.

4. Performance budget: target 60 FPS on mid-range hardware. Explain how you'll use instancing, frustum culling (Babylon does this natively), LOD, draw distance, object pooling for bullets/projectiles/particles, and requestAnimationFrame tuning.

5. Data-driven design: how enemies/weapons/levels are defined (config objects) so content can be tuned without code changes.

**C. SYSTEMS DETAIL**
1. Player controller: WASD + mouse-look (pointer lock), jump/crouch, sprint, weapon switch (1-4 keys), reload, shoot, health/armor/ammo, score, wave/level progression, kill streaks.
2. Enemy AI: perception (line-of-sight raycast), state transitions, pathing (simple: move toward player in 2D projected plane, avoid walls via steering), attack cooldowns, damage application, death/victory handling.
3. Combat: hit detection (raycast from weapon muzzle in weapon's forward direction), damage numbers, knockback, crits.
4. Projectiles: player bullets + enemy projectiles with physics, collision, trails.
5. Particles: muzzle flash, blood, fire, sparks, explosion.
6. Minimap: top-down projection of player + enemies with icons, updated each frame.
7. UI/HUD: health/armor/ammo bars, weapon name, score, wave info, crosshair, kill feed, level intro.
8. Audio: WebAudio synthesized SFX (no file deps) — gunshots, reload, footsteps, enemy roars, hits, deaths, powerup, BFG.
9. Save/load: localStorage for high score + best time.

**D. TESTING STRATEGY**
- Unit tests (what to test: collision, AI state machine, weapon damage math, audio synthesis) using a lightweight framework (e.g., Vitest or plain node asserts) — note that Babylon.js may need mocking.
- Playwright E2E tests (load the game, click to shoot, kill an enemy, verify score increments; open minimap; verify powerup pickup).
- Performance test: FPS measurement via requestAnimationFrame timing.

Report the spec as a well-organized markdown document. Be concrete with numbers (damage values, HP, fire rates, etc.) — I will implement from this spec. Do NOT write implementation code, only the spec.

[syntheticmagus](https://forum.babylonjs.com/u/syntheticmagus) January 6, 2022, 8:16pm 48

Good questions.

1. The `Input` class is just a bespoke encapsulation of Babylon’s new input system. I structured my encapsulation very similarly to Unity’s old `Input` class just for ease of use, but the basic idea is to encapsulate Babylon’s extremely general input system into a smaller contract that provides only the things you need for your specific scenario, thus allowing you the convenience of your own contract and calling conventions while still leveraging the Babylon-recommended way to get user input.
2. Ammo.
js is my physics engine of choice for a number of reasons, prominently support and stability: the library is actually [Bullet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_\(software\)) compiled to WebAssembly by [kripken](https://github.com/kripken/ammo.js) , one of the most prominent contributors to WebAssembly itself. Thus, Ammo.js has behind it one of the largest and most proficient communities of any open source physics engine. However, in this particular case it also had something else I needed that is, as far as I know, not possible in many other Web-usable physics engines: in lines 85 through 96, I reach through Babylon’s physics abstraction and into Ammo.js directly in order to selectively lock certain attributes of the underlying physics imposter, specifically rotation. This is necessary because the character controller needs to react physically in translation space (being knocked aside by the boxes, running into walls, etc.
) while simultaneously being unreactive in rotation space (otherwise the character controller would fall over). Again, this is a direct usage of features in Ammo.js which are not available in some other physics engines.
3. I’m not super familiar with Babylon’s built-in collision system, but my understanding of it is that it’s quite old, JavaScript-based, and really intended for simple scenarios. It is not, as I understand it, intended to be used in conjunction with a real physics engine because a physics engine must necessarily have its own collision system. Regarding perf, I would expect Ammo.js to be _much_ more performant (and feature-rich) for complex scenarios because (1) it’s a well-established full-featured physics engine with a huge support community and (2) it runs in WASM, which can provide _dramatic_ performance improvements over JavaScript for math-intensive operations. In short, I expect Ammo.
js to be much better suited to this task performance-wise than the default collision system because Babylon’s built-in collisions were never really intended to do this sort of thing, whereas full-on physics simulation is exactly what Ammo.js does best.

[syntheticmagus](https://forum.babylonjs.com/u/syntheticmagus) January 8, 2022, 1:46am 50

labris:
> What is the recommended way to use it with GLB levels models (where a ‘player’ is inside a model)?
> 
>

The short answer is that I don’t know yet, at least not for sure. This exact set of problems is part of what I’ll be exploring when we make [the golden path for the “walking simulator,”](https://forum.babylonjs.com/t/golden-paths-for-babylon-js/25935/5) likely shortly after 5.0 release. I can tell you that what I _think_ I’ll recommend is having specially-marked (by name or other mechanism) geometry in the glTF that the loading code can then find and turn into physics impostors. This will allow complete control of the collision system directly from the DCC tools used to produce the assets and remove the difficulties of trying to hand-craft physics entities in Babylon itself. However, I’ve not actually tried this, and it will likely be a few months before I get a chance to do so in the context of the “walking simulator” golden path.
That’s definitely on the radar, though!

Regarding using an `ArcRotateCamera` with physics collisions, my honest recommendation would be to not attempt it. I don’t really know what the desired behavior for such an interaction would be, but generally speaking I wouldn’t advocate trying to mix physics (which tries to control the behavior of objects) with Babylon’s utility cameras (which have highly specialized behaviors all of their own). If all you want to do is keep the camera centered on a character, you could probably use an `ArcRotateCamera` for that, but I wouldn’t try to add physics to it. If you want to make it avoid clipping through walls, your best bet is probably a per-frame raycast from the character toward the camera to determine the correct distance. If your environment is fully robust physics-wise (i.e., absolutely everything has an imposter) then that raycast might be done within the physics system; but if your physics environment is more sparse (i.e.
, impostors elided on high ceilings, etc. that players can’t collide with but cameras might), then it might be more appropriate to use Babylon’s built-in mesh-based collision system for that specific raycast.

Hope this helps, and best of luck!

# Optimizing Babylon.js Performance for the Web

Updated June 2026

Web game performance is constrained by the browser sandbox, shared GPU resources, JavaScript's single-threaded execution model, and the enormous variety of hardware that players use. Babylon.
js provides tools for each of these constraints: the Inspector for profiling, instancing for draw call reduction, octree partitioning for culling, KTX2 compression for textures, and the Scene Optimizer for adaptive quality. This guide covers how to identify bottlenecks and apply the right optimization for each one.

Learn AI engineering at Zero to Mastery

The first rule of optimization is to measure before you change anything. A game might feel slow because of excessive draw calls, oversized textures, unoptimized shaders, physics simulation overhead, garbage collection pauses, or simply too many polygons on screen. Each problem has a different solution, and applying the wrong optimization wastes development time without improving frame rate. Start with profiling, identify the bottleneck, apply the targeted fix, and measure again.

### Step 1: Profile Before Optimizing

The Babylon.js Inspector shows real-time statistics at a glance. Toggle it with `scene.debugLayer.show()` .
The statistics panel displays FPS, draw calls, active meshes, active vertices, active faces, frame time breakdown, and GPU memory estimates. This tells you immediately whether the bottleneck is CPU-side (too many JavaScript operations per frame) or GPU-side (too many pixels, vertices, or draw calls).

Chrome DevTools Performance tab provides deeper analysis. Record a few seconds of gameplay, then examine the flame chart. Long bars in the "Scripting" section indicate JavaScript is the bottleneck. Long bars in "Rendering" suggest too many draw calls. Long bars in "GPU" mean the graphics card is overloaded. Each finding leads to a different optimization strategy.

The `scene.getEngine().getFps()` method returns the current frame rate as a number. Log it periodically or display it as an on-screen counter during development. More useful is `scene.getLastFrameDuration()` , which returns the time in milliseconds for the last frame. If this number is consistently above 16.

...

For the farthest LOD level, consider using billboard impostors instead of 3D meshes. A billboard is a flat quad that always faces the camera, textured with a pre-rendered image of the object. At extreme distances, a billboard is indistinguishable from a 3D mesh but costs almost nothing to render. Babylon.js provides impostor rendering through the `SimplificationType` options.

### Step 4: Compress and Optimize Textures

Textures are typically the largest consumer of GPU memory. A single 2048x2048 RGBA texture uses 16MB uncompressed. Ten such textures consume 160MB, which exceeds the GPU memory budget on many mobile devices. KTX2 compression with Basis Universal reduces each texture to 2 to 4MB while maintaining visual quality, and the compressed data transcodes to the optimal GPU format at runtime.

Share materials between meshes whenever possible.

...

js generates mipmaps by default; do not disable them unless you have a specific reason.

### Step 5: Enable Scene Partitioning

Frustum culling determines which objects are visible to the camera and skips rendering for objects that are off screen. By default, Babylon.js tests every mesh against the camera frustum every frame. For scenes with thousands of objects, this linear scan becomes a bottleneck. Octree partitioning divides the scene into spatial regions so only objects in potentially visible regions need testing.

Create an octree with `scene.createOrUpdateSelectionOctree()` . The octree subdivides the scene bounding box into eight child boxes, and each child subdivides further up to a configurable depth. During culling, the engine tests the camera frustum against octree nodes rather than individual meshes. If an octree node is entirely outside the frustum, all meshes in that node are skipped without individual testing.

Octrees also accelerate picking (clicking on 3D objects).
Without spatial indexing, a pick ray test checks every mesh in the scene. With an octree, it only checks meshes in the spatial regions that the ray passes through. For scenes with complex geometry and frequent picking (RTS games, point-and-click adventures, editors), this reduces pick time from milliseconds to microseconds.

### Step 6: Configure the Scene Optimizer

The Scene Optimizer monitors frame rate and automatically adjusts rendering quality to maintain a target FPS. Create it with `BABYLON.SceneOptimizer.OptimizeAsync(scene, options, onSuccess, onFailure)` . The options define a sequence of optimizations to apply, from least visible to most impactful: reduce shadow map resolution, disable lens effects, lower texture resolution, remove particles, reduce post-processing quality, and finally lower the rendering resolution.

Custom optimization sequences let you prioritize what matters for your game.

...

Apply targeted fixes: instancing for draw calls, LOD for vertex count, KTX2 for texture memory, octrees for culling, and the Scene Optimizer for adaptive quality on unknown hardware.

## Support

Instances are supported for collisions, picking, rendering, and shadows. Even if the current hardware does not support hardware-accelerated instances, Babylon.js will still optimize rendering to take instances into account.

Starting from 5.0, instances that have a transparent material applied can be sorted from back to front to remove/limit rendering artifacts. This mode is enabled by setting `BABYLON.Mesh.INSTANCEDMESH_SORT_TRANSPARENT = true`.

Note that for performance sake the master mesh (the mesh from which instances are created by calling `masterMesh.
createInstance`) is not taken into account in the sorting process. So, to avoid rendering artifacts between this mesh and its instances, this mesh should be disabled (`masterMesh.setEnabled(false)`).

## What Are They?

In classic texturing, we use 2D images, often pictures that have been shaped specifically to match an object. Let’s imagine you are creating a medieval fantasy game, working on a dwarf pub, where there are multiple, big, "old school" wooden tables. With classic 2D texturing, you have 3 choices:
- Create a single texture and use it on all of the tables (but every table is going to look the same)

- Create a collection of various wood textures and apply them randomly to each table

- Create a separate texture for each table, insuring that they each look different

No choice seems to be a good one.

Enter **procedural textures**.

Procedural texturing is a way to programmatically create a texture. There are 2 types of procedural textures: code-only, and code that references some classic 2D images, sometimes called 'refMaps' or 'sampler' images.

One main advantage of procedural textures is that they are written using a fragment shader (using [GLSL](https://www.khronos.org/opengl/wiki/OpenGL_Shading_Language) in the case of Babylon.js). That means that the code generating the texture is executed by the GPU and not the CPU (that is to say, NOT executed in JavaScript code). This has a huge performance impact in a positive way.

Procedural textures can be generated:
- Only once to create the texture which is put into cache

- Every 1, 2, 3, or 4, or more frames to be able to create an animated texture (like fire)

See more about 'refresh rate' in the Custom Procedural Textures section... far below.

## Procedural Textures in Babylon.js

**Babylon.js** offers you an easy out-of-the-box way to use this kind of texture. The engine itself provides you with standard default textures that you can use right now. It also gives you the ability to create custom procedural textures and package them in a simple way.

## Using a Procedural Texture

Applying a procedural texture is just the same as using a classic one. Let’s start with a simple mesh (a cylinder in this case) and attach it to your scene:

```javascript
const cylinder = BABYLON.MeshBuilder.CreateCylinder("mycylinder", { height: 7, diameterTop: 2, diameterBottom: 2, tessellation: 12, subdivisions: 1 }, scene);
```

Then, you need to create a StandardMaterial:
```javascript
const material = new BABYLON.StandardMaterial("material", scene);
```

Now, create a WoodProceduralTexture object for which you need to pass a name, the size of the generated texture and the scene.

```javascript
const texture = new BABYLON.WoodProceduralTexture("texture", 1024, scene);
```

You are almost set! All you need to do now is to associate the texture to the material as a diffuseTexture, for instance, (or emissiveTexture, specularTexture, any other) and then apply the material to the mesh.

```javascript
material.diffuseTexture = texture;
cylinder.material = material;
```

You can optionally change the values of special default properties. Here is an example of setting two properties for the WoodProceduralTexture:

```javascript
texture.woodColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.49, 0.25, 0);
texture.ampScale = new BABYLON.Vector2(1.0, 1.0);
```

## Noise Procedural Texture
The NoiseProceduralTexture is available out of the box with the core Babylon.js engine.

You can create one with the following code:

```javascript
const noiseTexture = new BABYLON.NoiseProceduralTexture("perlin", 256, scene);
```

The NoiseProceduralTexture exposes the following properties:

- brightness: Gets or sets a value between 0 and 1 indicating the overall brightness of the texture (default is 0.2)
- octaves: Defines the number of octaves to process (default is 3)
- persistence: Defines the level of persistence (0.8 by default)
- animationSpeedFactor: Gets or sets animation speed factor (default is 1)

# Copies, Clones and Instances

In Babylon.js, creating copies of meshes can be achieved using different techniques depending on the needs and performance considerations of your scene. These techniques include **cloning, instancing, and thin instancing** . Each approach has its own use cases, especially when dealing with large numbers of objects or meshes with unique or shared properties.

* * *

## Clone 

A clone is a fully independent copy of a mesh.
The cloned mesh will have its own transformations (position, rotation, scaling), material, and geometry, but it starts off with the same values as the original mesh. Once cloned, you can modify the clone separately from the original.
To clone an element use `cloneFrom` prop:

```
<>     < box  name = 'box'  options = { {  width:  1.3 ,  height:  2 ,  depth:  0.7  } }  positionX = { - 1 } >         < standardMaterial  name = 'red-material'  diffuseColor = { Color3 . Red () }  />     </ box >     < box  name = 'cloned-box'  positionX = { 1 }  cloneFrom = 'box' >         < standardMaterial  name = 'yellow-material'  diffuseColor = { Color3 . Yellow () }  />     </ box > </>
```

If a Babylon.js element is clonable ( _Class.prototype.clone_ method exists), Reactylon will add `cloneFrom` prop to relative JSX element. Under the hood, Reactylon will call _.clone_ method to clone a specific element.

## Instance
An instance is a lightweight copy of a mesh that shares the same geometry and material as the original, but can have independent transformations (position, rotation, scale). Unlike cloning, instances use much less memory and are more efficient, as they share the geometry and material between the original mesh and all instances.
To create an instance of an element use `instanceFrom` prop:

```
<>     < box  name = 'box'  options = { {  width:  1.3 ,  height:  2 ,  depth:  0.7  } }  positionX = { - 1 }  >         < standardMaterial  name = 'red-material'  diffuseColor = { Color3 . Red () }  />     </ box >     < box  name = 'instanced-box'  positionX = { 1 }  instanceFrom = 'box' >         < standardMaterial  name = 'yellow-material'  diffuseColor = { Color3 . Yellow () }  />     </ box > </>
```

If a Babylon.js element is instanceable (only meshes), Reactylon will add `instanceFrom` prop to relative JSX element. Under the hood, Reactylon will call _.
createInstance_ method to create an instance starting from a specific element.

⚠️

In the above example we are attempting to assign a material ( _yellow-material_ ) to _instanced-box_ , since _instanced-box_ is an instance, it can not have its own material. Babylon.js will warn you that the operation has no effect with a warning in console.

* * *

A browser-based 3D first-person shooter inspired by the classic DOOM, built with vanilla JavaScript and raycasting.

## 🎯 Features

* **Raycasting 3D Engine** \- Classic pseudo-3D rendering like the original DOOM
* **Enemy AI** \- Intelligent enemies with patrol, chase, and attack behaviors
* **Combat System** \- Multiple weapons (Pistol, Shotgun, Rifle) with projectile-based shooting
* **Pickups** \- Health packs, ammo crates, and weapon upgrades scattered throughout the level
* **HUD** \- Real-time health, ammo, and weapon display
* **Win/Lose Conditions** \- Defeat all enemies to win, or lose if health reaches zero

## 🎮 How to Play

### Controls

|Key |Action |
| --- | --- |
|**W/A/S/D** |Move forward/left/backward/right |
|**Mouse** |Look around (360° rotation) |
|**Left Click** |Shoot |
|**1/2/3** |Switch weapons (Pistol/Shotgun/Rifle) |
|**ESC** |Pause game |

### Objective

Navigate through the level, eliminate all enemies, and collect pickups to survive!

### Gameplay Tips

* 🎯 **Click the screen** to lock mouse pointer and start playing
* 💊 **Green orbs** = Health packs (+25 HP)
* 📦 **Yellow orbs** = Ammo crates (+20 rounds)
* 🔫 **Cyan orbs** = Weapon upgrades (Shotgun)
* 🔴 **Red enemies** = Attacking, very dangerous!
* 🟠 **Orange enemies** = Patrolling or chasing
* 💥 **Shotgun** deals massive damage but uses 2 ammo per shot
* 🎯 **Aim for headshots** when enemies are close for maximum damage

## 🧠 Technical Details

### Raycasting Engine

The game uses a classic raycasting algorithm to create a pseudo-3D environment:

* **Field of View:** 60° (π/3 radians)
* **Resolution:** 320 rays cast per frame
* **Max render distance:** 20 tiles
* **Fish-eye correction:** Applied to prevent distortion

### Game Architecture

```
game.js
├── CONFIG           # Game constants (screen size, FOV, speeds)
├── Player System    # Movement, shooting, health, inventory
├── Enemy AI         # State machine (patrol/chase/attack)
├── Level Design     # 16x16 tile map with walls
├── Raycasting       # 3D rendering engine
├── Sprite System    # Billboard rendering for enemies/pickups
├── Collision        # Wall and entity collision detection
├── Projectiles      # Bullet physics and hit detection
└── Game Loop        # Main update/render cycle
```

### Map Layout

The level is a 16x16 grid where:

* `1` = Wall
* `0` = Empty space
* Enemies spawn at predefined positions
* Pickups are strategically placed throughout

```js
// Example map section (top-left corner)

**Mancubus** appear in _Doom 64_ . Their function in _Doom 64_ is unchanged to that in _Doom II_ .

The Mancubus of _Doom 64_ are the resurrected carcasses of those from Doom 1 (PSX or Saturn, since Mancubi don't appear in the original _Doom_ ), resurrected by the Mother Demon . They are made from systematically altered dead carnage remade back into corrupted living tissue. The mutations were devastating. The demons have returned stronger and more vicious than before.

[Sshot mancubus64](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/doom/images/b/b0/Sshot_mancubus64.png/revision/latest?cb=20100328125109) 

Mutations have greatly altered their apperance.
Their pupil-less eyes have blue sclera instead of green, their bodies have less fat and they a more bear-like face. They are taller and wear a metal body harness. Rather than a low growling sound when alerted, they will make a disgusting slobbering sound crescendoing into a low gutteral snarl. Their projectiles are smaller and appear more like fiery cannonballs. Their movement style popularly named "zombie gait" - body bobbing continually to the sides while walking, with both arms rigidly outstretched in front of its body - is very reminiscent of undead creatures in real-life vintage, undead-themed horror movies.

Despite being resurrected from decaying, dead tissue like other demons, the Doom 64 Mancubus is not quite as much as of a threat as they used to be. Their brimstone fireballs aren't shot in tricky-to-detect patterns to catch the player off guard, but instead each volley is shot straight at the player three times in succession.
Their smaller size also makes dodging them simpler. Fighting the Mancubus, like before, is best done with higher grade weapons, from the rocket launcher to the BFG to the souped-up Unmaker.

This type of Mancubus appears on the cover of an issue of _[Nintendo Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Power "wikipedia:Nintendo Power")_ featuring a spread of _Doom 64_ , including a two-page poster that features it in conjunction with other demons.

## README.md

# Babylon.js (babylon-js)

Babylon.js is an Apache-2.0 licensed, TypeScript-first open-source 3D engine and rendering framework sponsored by Microsoft and developed in the public BabylonJS GitHub organization. It targets WebGL, WebGPU, and WebXR in the browser, and DirectX, Metal, Vulkan, OpenGL, and OpenGL ES natively through Babylon Native — including a Babylon React Native binding for mobile.
The framework ships as a family of scoped npm packages plus a rich tooling surface — Playground, Sandbox, Inspector, Spector.js, the Node Material / Geometry / Particle / Render-Graph editors, a community Editor, the Babylon Toolkit (Unity / Unreal exporters), DCC exporters for 3ds Max / Maya / Blender, and a public Snippet API at `snippet.babylonjs.com` .

**URL:** [Visit APIs.json](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/api-evangelist/babylon-js/refs/heads/main/apis.yml)

### Babylon.js Sandbox

Drop-in browser viewer for 3D assets — glTF/GLB, OBJ, STL, USDZ, SPLAT, .babylon — with Inspector integration, IBL environment, and animation playback. The reference glTF viewer for the Babylon pipeline.

### Babylon.js Snippet API

Public REST endpoint at `https://snippet.babylonjs.com/` that stores and serves serialized JSON snippets for the Playground, Node Material Editor, Node Geometry Editor, Node Particle Editor, and GUI Editor. The same snippet IDs can be loaded at runtime via Babylon's snippet loaders to pull live assets into a scene.

C++ host that runs the Babylon.js engine on top of native graphics APIs (DirectX, Metal, Vulkan, OpenGL, OpenGL ES) without a browser. Targets Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS.

# DOOM64 — Browser Clone — Game Design Spec (v1.0)

> **Codename:** HELLRAISER
> **Engine:** Babylon.js 9.x (WebGL2, no build step, ES modules)
> **Delivery:** Single self-contained project, ZERO external asset downloads.
> **Target:** 60 FPS on mid-range hardware, < 1 MB total payload.

---

## 1. CORE ENGINE DECISION — Raycasting vs True 3D

**Decision: HYBRID.** Use a **Bresenham/Wolfenstein-style raycasting renderer** for the walls/floor/ceiling (authentic DOOM64 look, near-zero GPU cost), and a **Babylon.js 3D scene** for:
- Enemy 3D models (billboard-free, true meshes so enemies rotate/attack visibly)
- Weapons (first-person gun models that recoil/anim)
- Projectiles, particles, decals
- The minimap (2D canvas overlay)

**Why:** Pure raycasting (Piierai/doom-clone) renders great but enemies are sprites that can't do 3D attacks. Pure Babylon 3D is heavier. The hybrid gives DOOM64's iconic flat-shaded walls at ~320 rays/frame (60° FOV) while letting enemies/weapons be real 3D meshes. This is the architecturally correct choice for "runs without lagging."

**Collision:** Custom lightweight AABB + cylinder-vs-capsule collision (player capsule vs wall boxes). NOT a full physics engine (Havok/Ammo) — those add startup cost and complexity for no DOOM benefit. Player movement is integrated, not physics-driven.

---

## 2. CONTENT DESIGN — WEAPONS (4 required, 5 implemented)

| Weapon | RPM | Dmg/shot | Hitscan | Ammo | Reload (s) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Pistol** | 163.6 | 25 | Yes | 30 | 1.0 | 100% accurate, starter weapon |
| **Shotgun** | 56.8 | 35/beam (1-4 pellets) | Cone (60°) | 8 | 2.2 | Spread pattern, devastating close |

### 6.2 Enemy AI
- **Perception:** raycast from enemy to player; blocked by wall = lost LOS.

- **Sparks:** small fast particles on wall impact.

> **Codename:** HELLRAISER
> **Engine:** Babylon.js 9.x (WebGL2, no build step, ES modules)
> **Delivery:** Single self-contained project, ZERO external asset downloads.
> **Target:** 60 FPS on mid-range hardware, < 1 MB total payload.

## 1. CORE ENGINE DECISION — Raycasting vs True 3D

**Decision: HYBRID.** Use a **Bresenham/Wolfenstein-style raycasting renderer** for the walls/floor/ceiling (authentic DOOM64 look, near-zero GPU cost), and a **Babylon.js 3D scene** for:
- Enemy 3D models (billboard-free, true meshes so enemies rotate/attack visibly)
- Weapons (first-person gun models that recoil/anim)
- Projectiles, particles, decals
- The minimap (2D canvas overlay)

**Why:** Pure raycasting (Piierai/doom-clone) renders great but enemies are sprites that can't do 3D attacks. Pure Babylon 3D is heavier. The hybrid gives DOOM64's iconic flat-shaded walls at ~320 rays/frame (60° FOV) while letting enemies/weapons be real 3D meshes. This is the architecturally correct choice for "runs without lagging."

**Collision:** Custom lightweight AABB + cylinder-vs-capsule collision (player capsule vs wall boxes). NOT a full physics engine (Havok/Ammo) — those add startup cost and complexity for no DOOM benefit. Player movement is integrated, not physics-driven.

# DOOM64 Clone — Architecture Contract (v1.0)

> Companion to `DOOM64_SPEC.md`. Defines the **technical decisions**, **module interfaces**, and **integration contract** that executor agents must follow. Violating this contract = breaking coherence across tasks.

---

## 1. STACK (locked)

| Concern | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 3D engine | **Babylon.js 9.x** (ES module, global `BABYLON` via CDN import) | User-mandated. Mature, has PointerLockElement, ParticleSystem, CollisionEvent, instancing, octree, procedural textures. |
| Language | **TypeScript** (compiled to JS) | Type safety across a multi-agent codebase; Babylon is TS-first. |
| Build | **None.** Plain `npm run dev` (Vite dev server) serving the folder. | Self-contained, runs from any static host. |
| Rendering | **Hybrid:** raycasting (walls/floor/ceiling) + Babylon 3D (enemies/weapons/particles). | Authenticated decision in spec §1. |
| Collision | **Custom** AABB + capsule-vs-box. No Havok/Ammo. | Physics engines add startup + complexity for zero DOOM benefit. |
| Audio | **WebAudio synth.** No audio files. | Self-contained. |
| Tests | **Vitest** (unit) + **Playwright** (E2E). | Harness standard (R7/R29). |

> **CDN note:** Babylon core is loaded from `https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js` (the only external dependency, required for the engine itself). All *game* assets are generated procedurally — no art/model/sound files.

---

## 2. GLOBAL TYPES (`src/types.ts`) — shared vocabulary

```ts
// Vector math (reuse THREE.Vector3 via @babylonjs/core? No — use BABYLON.Vector3)
export type Vec3 = BABYLON.Vector3;
export type Vec2 = { x: number; y: number; };

// World coordinates
export interface Position { x: number; y: number; z: number; }   // y = up

// Enemy base interface (all enemies implement this)
export interface IEnemy {
  id: string;
  position: Vec3;
  health: number;
  maxHealth: number;
  speed: number;              // units/sec
  state: AIState;             // SLEEP|WAKE|CHASE|ATTACK|DEAD
  attackCooldown: number;     // seconds until next attack
  isBoss: boolean;
  takeDamage(amount: number): void;   // applies damage, may kill
  update(dt: number, playerPos: Vec3, playerHeading: Vec3): void;  // AI tick
  render(scene: BABYLON.Scene): void;
  dispose(): void;
}

// Enemy subtypes (Zombie, Imp, Demon, Cacodemon, Mancubus, Baron, HellKnight) extend IEnemy.

// Weapon interface
export interface IWeapon {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  maxAmmo: number;
  currentAmmo: number;
  fireRateRPM: number;
  damage: number;
  reloadTime: number;         // seconds
  type: 'hitscan' | 'cone' | 'projectile';
  spreadDegrees?: number;
  overheats?: boolean;        // chaingun
  maxOverheat?: number;       // 1.0 = overheated
  fire(origin: Vec3, dir: Vec3): void;
  canFire(now: number): boolean;   // rate + overheat gate
  reload(now: number): boolean;    // returns true if finished
}

// Game state (top-level)
export type GameState = 'MENU' | 'PLAYING' | 'PAUSED' | 'GAMEOVER' | 'VICTORY';

// Level grid value
export type Tile = 0 | 1 | 2;  // 0 empty, 1 wall, 2 door
```

---

## 3. MODULE INTERFACES (integration contract)

### 3.1 `InputManager` (input/InputManager.ts)
- **Constructor:** `new InputManager(engine: BABYLON.Engine, canvas: HTMLCanvasElement)`.
- **Methods:** `onKeyDown(key: string)`, `onKeyUp(key: string)`, `onMouseMove(dx: number, dy: number)`, `onMouseDown(button: string)`, `requestPointerLock()`, `isDown(key: string): boolean`.
- **Contract:** writes to an internal `keyState: Record<string, boolean>` map; exposes `movementVector()` (WASD → {x,z}) and `lookDelta()` (mouse → yaw/pitch radians). Pointer lock on click; releases on Escape.

### 3.2 `World` (world/World.ts)
- **Constructor:** `new World(scene, grid: number[][], width, height, tileUnit)`.
- **Builds:** floor plane, ceiling plane, wall boxes (one BABYLON.Box per wall cell), spawn points.
- **Methods:** `isWall(x, z): boolean` (AABB test), `nearestWall(x, z): Vec3`, `getSpawnPoints(): Vec3[]`, `render(scene)`.
- **Contract:** wall boxes carry `collidable = true` and a `tileType` property for collision + door detection.

### 3.3 `Collision` (world/Collision.ts)
- **Functions (pure, testable):** `resolveCapsuleWall(pos, radius, walls): Vec3`, `resolveEnemyWall(pos, radius, walls): Vec3`, `playerHitsWall(pos, radius, walls): boolean`.
- **Contract:** returns a NEW position (never mutates input). Walls from `World`.

### 3.4 `Player` (player/Player.ts)
- **Constructor:** `new Player(scene, input, world, config)`.
- **State:** position, velocity, health, armor, ammo[], score, kills, heading.
- **Methods:** `update(dt)`, `takeDamage(amount)`, `heal(amount)`, `addArmor(amount)`, `pickUp(kind)`, `switchWeapon(id)`, `shoot()`.
- **Contract:** `shoot()` delegates to the active `Weapon` and spawns projectiles/hitscan. Emits damage to enemies via `Combat`.

### 3.5 `Weapon` (weapons/Weapon.ts + subtypes)
- **Base:** `new Weapon(scene, config)`. Manages ammo, rate, overheat.
- **`fire(origin, dir)`** spawns a `Projectile` (projectile type) or calls `Combat.hitscan()` / spawns cone pellets.
- **`canFire(now)`** enforces RPM + overheat gate. **`reload(now)`** decrements reload timer.
- **Contract:** weapons are data-driven from `config/weapons.ts`; no per-weapon code beyond behavior differences.

### 3.6 `Enemy` (entities/Enemy.ts + subtypes)
- **Base:** `new Enemy(scene, type, spawnPos, config)`. Holds `IEnemy` contract.
- **AI:** runs `AIState` FSM. `update(dt, playerPos, playerHeading)` handles perception → state transition → movement → attack.
- **`takeDamage(amount)`** from `Player.shoot()`: decrements health, spawns `ParticleFX.blood()`, on death spawns debris + `DamageNumber` + score.
- **Subtypes** override defaults: Cacodemon adds teleport, Mancubus throws 3 fireballs, Baron is tanky, Boss implements `Boss` multi-phase.

### 3.7 `AIState` (ai/AIState.ts)
- **Enum:** `SLEEP | WAKE | CHASE | ATTACK | DEAD`.
- **`decide(state, playerPos, playerHeading, dt)`** → next action or keep. Uses LOS raycast (throttled ≤2Hz via `lastLosCheck`).
- **Contract:** pure decision function, testable in isolation.

### 3.8 `Combat` (combat/Combat.ts)
- **`hitscan(origin, dir, enemies): IEnemy | null`** — raycast against enemy list, returns nearest hit.
- **`spawnProjectile(type, origin, dir, damage)`** — pools a `Projectile`.
- **`applyExplosion(pos, radius, damage)`** — sphere damage + knockback + `ParticleFX.fire()`.
- **`spawnDamageNumber(enemy, amount, crit)`** — floating text.

### 3.9 `ParticleFX` (particles/ParticleFX.ts)
- **Wrappers:** `muzzleFlash(weaponMesh)`, `blood(enemy)`, `fire(pos)`, `explosion(pos)`, `sparks(pos)`.
- **Contract:** uses `BABYLON.ParticleSystem`; respects a global `particleBudget` cap; `restart()` on dispose.

### 3.10 `AssetGen` (assets/AssetGen.ts)
- **Procedural textures:** `brickTexture()`, `floorTexture()`, `wallFlat(color)`, `bloodDecal()`. Canvas-based or shader-based (GPU). Max 256×256.
- **Model builders:** `buildWeaponModel(kind)`, `buildEnemyModel(kind)`, `buildBossModel()`, `buildCrate()`. Box/cylinder composites.
- **Contract:** zero external loads; returns `BABYLON.Material`/`BABYLON.Mesh`.

### 3.11 `Audio` (assets/Audio.ts)
- **`init()`** creates `AudioContext`. **`play(kind)`** synthesizes: ` gunshot|reload|footstep|roar|hit|death|powerup|bfg|music`.
- **Contract:** no files; `mute`/`unmute`; panning via `PannerNode`, volume via `GainNode`.

### 3.12 `Minimap` (minimap/Minimap.ts)
- **Constructor:** `new Minimap(canvas, world, player, enemies)`.
- **`update()`** each frame: draw grid, player triangle (heading), enemy squares, pickup circles.
- **Contract:** reads same transform data as 3D render (single source of truth).

### 3.13 `Hud` (ui/Hud.ts)
- **Constructor:** `new Hud(rootEl)`.
- **`update(player, weapon)`** — redraws health/armor/ammo bars, ammo count, score, kill feed.
- **`showMenu(state)`** — MENU/PAUSED/GAMEOVER/VICTORY overlays.
- **Contract:** HTML/CSS overlay; no Babylon GUI dependency.

### 3.14 `GameState` (state/GameState.ts)
- **`new GameState(scene, input, player, world, enemies, hud, audio)`**.
- **`setState(s)`** transitions; `update(dt)` dispatches to subsystems only when `PLAYING`.
- **Contract:** owns the frame loop delegation; guards that input/enemies only tick when playing.

### 3.15 `main-loop.ts`
- **`run()`** — `BABYLON.Engine` + `scene` setup, then `scene.onBeforeRenderRender` → `GameState.update(dt)` → `scene.render()`.
- **Contract:** the single entry point; wires everything. Raycasting render happens inside `World.render`.

---

## 4. DATA-DRIVEN CONFIG (no per-level/per-enemy code)

- `config/weapons.ts`: array of weapon definitions → `Weapon` factory.
- `config/enemies.ts`: array of enemy definitions (HP, speed, attack, state params) → `Enemy` factory.
- `config/levels.ts`: grid arrays + spawn/pickup JSON per map → `World` factory.
- **Rule:** adding a weapon/enemy/level = editing config JSON, NOT new code. Executor agents may add new *behavior* (e.g., chaingun overheat) but must not hardcode per-instance logic.

---

## 5. DEPENDENCY DIRECTION

```
config/*, types.ts  (no deps)
   ↑
input, world, assets, ai  (depend on config/types)
   ↑
player, weapons, entities, combat, particles  (depend on above)
   ↑
minimap, ui, state  (depend on all subsystems)
   ↑
main-loop  (depends on state)
```
No cycles. Testable modules (Collision, AIState, weapons) have NO Babylon dependency → pure unit tests.

---

## 6. QUALITY BARS

- **Code:** < 50 lines/functions per file where possible; no `console.log`; errors handled; no hardcoded secrets.
- **Tests:** unit coverage ≥ 80% on `Collision`, `AIState`, `weapons`, `Player` math. Playwright E2E: shoot→kill→score→minimap→pickup all pass.
- **Perf:** ≥ 50 FPS sustained with 8 enemies + boss. Draw calls minimized via instancing/octree.
- **Security (R6):** no eval of untrusted input; no DOM injection from data; audio context user-gesture gated.

---

## 7. IMPLEMENTATION ORDER (dependency-respecting waves)

1. **Foundation:** types, config, InputManager, World, Collision, AssetGen, Audio.
2. **Core loop:** main-loop, GameState, Player, Weapon base.
3. **Combat:** Combat (hitscan/projectile/explosion), DamageNumber.
4. **Enemies:** AIState, Enemy base, 6 subtypes.
5. **FX/UI:** ParticleFX, Minimap, Hud.
6. **Boss + levels + polish:** Boss subtype, remaining levels, powerups, save/load.
7. **Tests:** unit (Vitest) + E2E (Playwright).

# DOOM64 Clone — Implementation Plan (v1.0)

- **Test:** `tests/particles.test.ts` — systems create particles; budget cap respected; restart reuses.

### T17: Minimap (2D canvas)

- **Test:** `tests/minimap.test.ts` — player position drawn; enemy appears after spawn; pickup circle after pickup.

### T18: Hud
- `src/ui/Hud.ts`: health/armor/ammo bars, ammo count, score, kill feed, MENU/PAUSED/GAMEOVER/VICTORY overlays. HTML/CSS.
- **Contract:** §3.13.
- **Test:** `tests/hud.test.ts` — bars update with health; ammo count changes; gameover overlay shows.

### T19: Boss (multi-phase)
- `src/entities/Boss.ts`: 2400HP, 3 phases, invulnerable windows, escalating attacks (melee→fireballs+slam→dash+firestorm), Soul Stone on death.

- **Test:** `tests/boss.test.ts` — phase transitions at 66%/33% HP; invulnerable during window; each attack reduces player HP.

- **Contract:** spec §6.9.

- Level factory from config; spawn enemies/pickups; level intro banner; win on boss death.
- **Contract:** spec §5.
- **Test:** `tests/level.test.ts` — level loads with enemies at spawn points; boss death → victory state.

Context: Building a DOOM64 browser clone at `/mnt/dados/projetos/doom/`. You are implementing ONE atomic task (T1). Read the design spec and contract BEFORE writing code.

Read these files first (they contain the full design + module interfaces):
- `/mnt/dados/projetos/doom/DOOM64_SPEC.md`
- `/mnt/dados/projetos/doom/DOOM64_CONTRACT.md`

**YOUR TASK (T1): Project scaffold + types + config**

Create these files:
1. `index.html` — entry point with `<canvas id="renderCanvas">`, `<div id="hud">` root, and `<script type="module" src="./src/main.ts">`. Include Babylon CDN import in main.ts. DOOM64 4-color aesthetic (red/orange/black/cream).
2. `style.css` — HUD styling: health bar (red, bottom-left), armor bar (blue), ammo (bottom-center), score (top-right), kill feed, crosshair, menus. Font: monospace/DOOM-like.
3. `vite.config.ts` — Vite dev server config (no build needed, just serves the folder). base: './'.
4. `package.json` — dependencies: `babylonjs@9`, dev: `typescript`, `vite`, `vitest`, `playwright`, `@types/node`. Scripts: `dev`, `build`, `test`, `e2e`.
5. `tsconfig.json` — TypeScript config for ES modules, Babylon types.
6. `src/types.ts` — shared types: `Vec3 = BABYLON.Vector3`, `Vec2 = {x:number;y:number}`, `Position`, `AIState` enum (SLEEP|WAKE|CHASE|ATTACK|DEAD), `IEnemy` interface (id, position, health, maxHealth, speed, state, attackCooldown, isBoss, takeDamage(amount), update(dt, playerPos, playerHeading), render(scene), dispose()), `IWeapon` interface (id, name, maxAmmo, currentAmmo, fireRateRPM, damage, reloadTime, type: 'hitscan'|'cone'|'projectile', spreadDegrees?, overheats?, maxOverheat?), `GameState` type ('MENU'|'PLAYING'|'PAUSED'|'GAMEOVER'|'VICTORY'), `Tile` type (0|1|2).
7. `src/config/weapons.ts` — array of 5 weapon definitions: pistol (163.6 RPM, 25 dmg, 30 ammo, 1.0s reload, hitscan, 100% accurate), shotgun (56.8 RPM, 35 dmg, 8 ammo, 2.2s reload, cone 60deg), chaingun (530 RPM, 9 dmg, 50 ammo, 2.4s reload, hitscan, overheats=true, maxOverheat=1.0), rocket (40 RPM, 200 dmg splash 40u radius, 20 ammo, 2.5s reload, projectile), bfg (56 RPM, 2060 dmg, 1 ammo, 3.0s reload, hitscan, needs BFG Cell). Each: {id, name, maxAmmo, currentAmmo, fireRateRPM, damage, reloadTime, type, spreadDegrees?, overheats?, maxOverheat?}.
8. `src/config/enemies.ts` — array of 7 enemy definitions: zombie (100HP, 40u/s, melee claw 25, drops ammo), imp (60HP, 60u/s, fireball 20, melee), demon (120HP, 80u/s, fireball 35), cacodemon (400HP, 80u/s, teleport 12u, lunge), mancus (600HP, 60u/s, 3 fireballs), baron (800HP, 50u/s, melee 40), hellknight (500HP, 70u/s, green fireball). Each: {id, name, hp, maxHealth, speed, attackDamage, attackRange, attackInterval, type, isBoss, teleportRange?, fireballCount?, special?}.
9. `src/config/levels.ts` — MAP1 "The Armory" (24x24 grid, tutorial, 6 zombies + 2 imps), MAP2 "The Catacombs" (30x30, 4 demons + 2 mancus + 3 barons), MAP3 "The Mother Chamber" (32x32 arena, 2 cacodemons + 2 hellknights + boss). Each map: {name, grid: number[][], width, height, tileUnit, enemySpawns: {x,z,type}[], pickups: {x,z,kind}[]}. Grid: 0=empty, 1=wall, 2=door.
10. `tests/config.test.ts` — Vitest test: every weapon has id/name/maxAmmo/fireRateRPM/damage/reloadTime/type; every enemy has id/name/hp/maxHealth/speed/attackDamage/attackRange; every grid is rectangular (all rows same length = width).

**STRICT RULES:**
- TypeScript, ES modules, comments in pt-BR.
- No `console.log` anywhere.
- No external asset files — only Babylon CDN.
- Keep files small (< 200 lines each).
- Make config arrays DATA-DRIVEN (the Weapon/Enemy/World factories will read these).
- After writing, run `npm test` and confirm the config tests PASS.
- Report: list of files created + test results.
